analysis.one_liner: Bars private student lenders from demanding full repayment when a loan's cosigner dies or becomes disabled.
analysis.headline: The bill never moved after a House committee received it, and it died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal lending law to stop private student loan companies from invoking a little-known clause that lets them demand the full loan balance immediately when a cosigner dies or becomes permanently disabled, even if the borrower is paying on time. It was introduced by one House member, sent to the Financial Services Committee, and never taken up. It expired when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who are current on private student loans but whose cosigner, usually a parent, dies or becomes disabled. Under the bill, lenders could no longer call the entire loan due in that situation, so a family would not suddenly owe the full balance because of a death or serious injury.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers paying private student loans on time

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a private educational lender from accelerating the repayment terms of an outstanding loan when a jointly liable cosigner dies or becomes disabled, so long as the borrower is in good standing.
Defines disability to include permanent and total disability under Education Department rules, or a Veterans Affairs determination that a person is unemployable due to a service-connected condition.

analysis.who_pays: Private student loan companies, which would lose the ability to demand full immediate repayment on loans where the cosigner — often a parent or relative who served as the credit backing — dies or becomes disabled. They would instead carry the borrower's continuing payment schedule.

drawbacks.text: Lenders point out that the cosigner's credit is often why the loan was made at all; taking away the right to accelerate the loan after a cosigner's death or disability leaves them holding more risk, which they may price into higher rates or tighter credit for other borrowers.

The bill leaves 'good standing' to be determined by regulation by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rather than fixing it in law, which adds a rulemaking process and some uncertainty for both borrowers and lenders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is narrow but real: it targets a specific harsh contract clause, automatic acceleration on a cosigner's death or disability, and only for borrowers who are current on payments. The cost to lenders is a modest increase in risk on those loans, which could show up as slightly higher rates or stricter underwriting. On balance the bill trades a small, spread-out cost for removing an abrupt financial blow to families at the worst possible moment.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Daniel Kildee introduced the bill on September 8, 2015 and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
No other member cosponsored the bill, and no further action of any kind appears in its record after the referral.
The bill died without a committee vote or a floor vote when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student loan lenders are better off because the bill died; nothing changed, so they kept the contractual right to demand full repayment when a cosigner dies or becomes disabled.

for.name: Rep. Daniel Kildee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; no one else signed on.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.role: Committee of referral for Truth in Lending Act bills
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after it was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record.

against.name: Rep. Jeb Hensarling
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the two years it sat in the committee.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member sponsored the bill, so the record shows too little participation to tell how support would have split by party; the committee that sat on it was run by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would take away their right to demand the full loan balance immediately when a cosigner dies or becomes disabled, even while the borrower pays on time. That protection would have fallen on grieving families; keeping it means the lenders' gain comes at those families' expense.
